Topic: What is the fair rate of interest to charge our grandchildren for the carbon we are borrowing from their atmosphere today?
Montaigne — Judgement:
Men can indeed put their toes together, but not their heads — and this is such a case, where our reasoning is stretched to serve an appetite our senses cannot feel. I have written that of all follies, none is greater than wanting to reform the world for a posterity we shall never meet, upon a promise we ourselves would not honor if presented the reverse.

The question of "fair rate" presupposes we are lenders acting in good conscience, when in truth we are debtors who have already spent the principal and now haggle over the receipt. My essay on repentance taught me that we judge each action in its moment, stripped of the comfort of later accounting — and this atmosphere is borrowed the way a drunkard borrows from tomorrow's sober self: not at a rate, but as theft dressed in the vocabulary of finance.

There is no honest rate of interest for a debt we intend never to repay in the currency we took it in.

*We do not borrow from our grandchildren — we simply steal, and call the theft a loan so that our own conscience may sleep.*
Austen — Judgement:
I have always held that an estate mismanaged by one generation becomes a mortgage upon the next, and the atmosphere is precisely such an estate — entailed to heirs who never signed the settlement.

The question assumes a negotiation, but Sir Walter Elliot did not negotiate with Anne when he let Kellynch's rents run behind his vanity; he merely spent, and called the spending taste. We speak of "interest" as though our grandchildren were creditors we might charm with agreeable terms, when in truth they are wards, and we the guardians drawing upon a trust we did not create and cannot replenish. A rate implies consent on both sides; here the only consenting party is the one not yet born.

There is no fair rate of interest on a debt contracted without the debtor's knowledge — the only honest arithmetic is to stop borrowing.

*A gentleman who lives on his heir's income has not discovered credit — he has discovered a genteel word for theft.*
Bashō — Judgement:
The very framing—"interest rate," "borrowing," a ledger stretching to grandchildren—is the sickness, not the cure. I spent my life walking toward Ōgaki with nothing, learning that the moon does not accrue value by being watched twice.

To ask what rate is fair is to imagine the atmosphere as capital we may prudently manage across generations. But I saw at Matsushima that even islands famous for a thousand years dissolve in the telling of them; nothing holds still long enough to be owed. We are not creditors of tomorrow's air, we are guests in this hour's air, and guests who wreck the house cannot repay their host with a schedule of payments—only by leaving before more damage is done.

There is no fair interest rate, because carbon debt is not a loan but a theft from the unrepeatable now, and it is settled only by stopping, not by financing the theft more gently.

*A borrowed sky cannot be repaid in coin—only in the traveler's discipline of taking less than he needs.*
Emerson — Judgement:
The question assumes a ledger between generations, as though the atmosphere were a bank and we its solvent borrowers — but Nature keeps no such polite accounts.

My law of Compensation teaches that every debt is paid, in kind, without discount, and without our leave to set the terms. We call it "borrowing" carbon only to flatter ourselves that repayment is optional, deferred, a matter for actuaries to haggle over — but the sky does not lend; it simply records, and the record becomes weather, becomes drought, becomes the fever of children not yet named. The self-reliant man does not spend what another must be taxed to repay; a generation that lives so has not truly lived, only postponed the reckoning onto hands too small to refuse it.

There is no fair rate of interest on a debt we had no right to incur, for the true rate is compensation in full, exacted whether we consent or not.

*Nature holds no debtors' prison — only a harvest, and it comes due to whoever is standing in the field.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
Every age fancies it may govern the next, and every age is a fool for it. I said in the *Rights of Man* that the earth belongs in usufruct to the living, and no generation has the right to mortgage the choices of one not yet born. The carbon we burn today is not a loan we contracted — it is a trespass we commit against an heir who never signed the deed and cannot refuse the bill. To speak of "interest" is to dignify theft with the language of finance; a debt owed to someone who never consented to lend is not a debt at all, it is plunder deferred. There is no rate of interest that makes a stolen inheritance honest — only restitution does that, paid now, in carbon left in the ground, not promises left on a ledger.

*A generation that spends its grandchildren's air is not borrowing — it is robbing, and calling the theft a loan does not make it a loan.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
The economy borrows from a debtor who has no lawyer in the room, no vote at the table, and no name on the ledger — my grandchildren, mortgaged in absentia.

The question mistakes theft for a loan, and a loan implies a rate of interest reasonable men might negotiate. But rights are not commodities to be discounted across time, and I have never accepted that duty diminishes with distance — I said of women what I now say of the unborn: subjection dressed as natural order is still subjection, only softened by sentiment. There is no rate at which it becomes just to let one generation's comfort compound as another's ruin. Justice is not a market; it does not clear.

There is no fair rate — the very idea of pricing their inheritance is the injustice, not its solution.

*A debt owed to those without a voice is not credit — it is tyranny wearing the mask of arithmetic.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
I have long argued that our sentiments run warm for what is near and grow faint for what is distant—a man will sleep soundly the night after learning of an earthquake that swallowed a hundred million strangers in China, yet lie awake over an aching finger of his own. The carbon we borrow is owed to persons whose distress we cannot feel at all, for they do not yet exist; our natural sympathy, left to itself, will always underprice their injury. But justice is not beneficence—it does not wait upon fellow-feeling. It is a matter of exact and indispensable rule, owed whether or not our hearts are moved. A prudent man does not compensate his creditor at the rate his indifference suggests, but at the rate that makes the creditor whole.

We must charge ourselves nearly nothing for delay and nearly everything for the debt itself: a near-zero discount rate, full restitution owed regardless of sentiment.

*Justice asks not what we feel for the unborn, but what we owe them.*
